ayahLayers.grammar: A rhetorical question is formed by أَ attached to رَأَيْتَ, followed by a relative phrase: ٱلَّذِى يُكَذِّبُ بِٱلدِّينِ. The relative clause identifies the person being considered.
ayahLayers.contextualMeaning: Have you considered the one who denies the Judgment or recompense?
sentenceMap: أَ + رَأَيْتَ: rhetorical question, Have you considered?
ٱلَّذِى يُكَذِّبُ بِٱلدِّينِ: the one who denies the Judgment or recompense

teaching.rootPicture: The root ر-أ-ي centers on seeing, and by extension considering or recognizing.
teaching.construction: أَ + رَأَيْتَ: an interrogative hamza attached to the perfect verb رَأَى.
teaching.grammar: The verb is perfect, second person masculine singular; the initial أَ turns the clause into a question.
teaching.sentenceRole: Main verb of the rhetorical question; the following relative phrase is what the listener is asked to consider.
teaching.recognitionClue: An initial أَ before a verb often signals a yes-or-no question; the ending تَ marks you, masculine singular, in the perfect tense.

forms.difference: The attached أَ changes the verb into a question asking the listener to consider the case.

teaching.takeaway: Read أَرَءَيْتَ as a prompt to reflect: Have you considered?

layers.occurrenceRole: Main verb of the rhetorical question.

features: weak final root radical in the lemma
morphology.notes: The interrogative hamza is written attached to the perfect verb; the context supports the sense Have you considered? rather than only the literal Have you seen?

layers.grammar: Interrogative أَ is prefixed to a perfect second-person masculine singular verb.
learnerConnections: Recognize أَ at the beginning of a verb as a common interrogative marker.
Connect the ending تَ with a masculine singular you-form in the perfect tense.

pedagogy.recognitionClue: Look first for the opening أَ, then read رَأَيْتَ as you saw/considered.
pedagogy.explanation: The Quranic spelling joins the question marker to the verb, so the full word begins with a question even though the verb itself is رَأَيْتَ.

teaching.rootPicture: Rootless grammatical word: learn ٱلَّذِى as a fixed relative pronoun rather than searching for a triliteral root.
teaching.construction: ٱلَّذِى is a fixed relative-pronoun form that introduces a describing clause.
teaching.grammar: Definite relative pronoun, masculine singular; it introduces يُكَذِّبُ بِٱلدِّينِ and refers to the person being considered.
teaching.sentenceRole: Introduces the relative clause that identifies the person under discussion.
teaching.recognitionClue: The fixed form ٱلَّذِى commonly means who or that for one masculine referent.
teaching.takeaway: ٱلَّذِى links a noun or person to the clause that describes it: the one who...

layers.occurrenceRole: Relative-clause marker referring to the person being considered.

morphology.notes: This is a fixed grammatical word with no productive triliteral root for learner analysis.

layers.grammar: Masculine singular relative pronoun introducing the clause يُكَذِّبُ بِٱلدِّينِ.
learnerConnections: Recognize ٱلَّذِى as the singular masculine counterpart of a relative-pronoun pattern.
Use the following verb clause to identify the person introduced by ٱلَّذِى.

pedagogy.recognitionClue: When ٱلَّذِى appears, expect a describing clause immediately after it.
pedagogy.explanation: It does not name an action by itself; it opens the who/that clause that follows.

teaching.rootPicture: The root ك-ذ-ب is associated with lying and treating a claim as false.
teaching.construction: Form II imperfect: the initial ي marks the third-person masculine singular, and the doubled middle radical is visible in ذِّ.
teaching.grammar: Imperfect indicative, active voice, third person masculine singular, Form II; it agrees with the masculine singular relative pronoun ٱلَّذِى.
teaching.sentenceRole: Predicate of the relative clause introduced by ٱلَّذِى.
teaching.recognitionClue: The initial ي marks a third-person imperfect verb, while the doubled middle consonant signals the Form II pattern.

forms.difference: Form II كَذَّبَ intensifies or causes the idea, giving deny or declare false rather than simply lie.

teaching.takeaway: يُكَذِّبُ describes an ongoing act of rejecting something as false.

layers.occurrenceRole: Predicate of the relative clause; its complement is بِٱلدِّينِ.

morphology.notes: The shadda on ذ is a visible clue to the doubled middle radical of Form II.

layers.grammar: Imperfect indicative, third person masculine singular, active Form II verb agreeing with ٱلَّذِى.
learnerConnections: Connect initial يـ with a third-person masculine singular imperfect verb.
Use the doubled middle consonant to recognize the Form II pattern.

pedagogy.recognitionClue: Find يـ at the front and the shadda on ذ in the middle.
pedagogy.explanation: The word is not simply lie: the Form II pattern presents the subject as declaring the following matter false.

teaching.rootPicture: The root د-ي-ن is associated with debt, judgment, and recompense; this context points to accountability before God.
teaching.construction: بِ + ٱل + دِينِ: a preposition joined to the definite noun دِينِ.
teaching.grammar: بِ is a preposition, so the definite masculine singular noun after it is genitive; the phrase is attached to يُكَذِّبُ.
teaching.sentenceRole: Prepositional complement specifying what is denied.
teaching.recognitionClue: Initial بِ often marks the matter a verb is directed toward, and the final kasra on دِينِ signals genitive in this occurrence.
teaching.takeaway: بِٱلدِّينِ identifies the matter being denied: the Judgment or recompense.

layers.occurrenceRole: Prepositional complement of يُكَذِّبُ, specifying what is denied.

morphology.notes: The sun-letter pronunciation of the article before د is represented in the preserved canonical spelling ٱلدِّينِ; the learner breakdown keeps the article as a meaningful component.

layers.grammar: بِ is a preposition followed by the definite noun دِينِ in the genitive, forming a complement to يُكَذِّبُ.
learnerConnections: Recognize بِ as a preposition that attaches directly to the following word.
Notice that a preposition makes the following noun genitive, shown here by the final kasra.

pedagogy.recognitionClue: Split the word as بِ + ٱل + دِّينِ and let the final kasra remind you of the preposition.
pedagogy.explanation: The phrase can be translated as concerning the Judgment or recompense; the exact English noun depends on the intended contextual emphasis.
pedagogy.takeaway: بِٱلدِّينِ = the Judgment/recompense as the object of denial

ayahLayers.grammar: فَ links the statement as a consequence or identification. ذَٰلِكَ is a demonstrative subject, and ٱلَّذِى يَدُعُّ ٱلْيَتِيمَ identifies it through a relative clause whose verb takes ٱلْيَتِيمَ as a direct object.
ayahLayers.contextualMeaning: That is the one who repulses the orphan.
sentenceMap: فَ: so / then, linking this statement to the preceding description
ذَٰلِكَ ٱلَّذِى...: that is the one who...

teaching.meaning: so that is the one / that person
teaching.rootPicture: Both pieces are rootless grammatical words: فَ links the statement, while ذَٰلِكَ points to a masculine singular referent.
teaching.construction: فَ + ذَٰلِكَ: a consequence connector written directly before the demonstrative.
teaching.grammar: فَ is a linking particle; ذَٰلِكَ is a masculine singular demonstrative pronoun functioning as the subject of the nominal structure.
teaching.sentenceRole: Connects the identification to ayah 1 and points back to the person just described.
teaching.recognitionClue: An attached فَ often means so/then; ذَٰلِكَ is the familiar that masculine singular form.
teaching.takeaway: فَذَٰلِكَ turns the previous description into an identification: so that is the one...

layers.occurrenceRole: Consequence connector plus demonstrative subject pointing back to the person in ayah 1.

morphology.notes: The two grammatical units are meaningfully separable even though the connector is written attached.

layers.grammar: فَ links the clause to what precedes; ذَٰلِكَ is a masculine singular demonstrative subject.
layers.meaning: so that is the one / that person
learnerConnections: Recognize attached فَ as a connector meaning so or then.
Recall ذَٰلِكَ as the masculine singular demonstrative that.

pedagogy.recognitionClue: Read the first two letters as فَ = so, then identify ذَٰلِكَ = that one.
pedagogy.explanation: The word points back to the person described in the previous ayah instead of introducing a new person.
pedagogy.takeaway: فَذَٰلِكَ = so that is the one

teaching.rootPicture: Rootless grammatical word: learn ٱلَّذِى as a fixed relative pronoun rather than searching for a triliteral root.
teaching.construction: ٱلَّذِى is a fixed relative-pronoun form that introduces a describing clause.
teaching.grammar: Masculine singular relative pronoun; here it identifies ذَٰلِكَ and introduces يَدُعُّ ٱلْيَتِيمَ.
teaching.sentenceRole: Identifying predicate/complement of ذَٰلِكَ and marker of the relative clause.
teaching.recognitionClue: The fixed form ٱلَّذِى commonly means who or that for one masculine referent.
teaching.takeaway: ٱلَّذِى links the demonstrative to the clause that tells which person it is.

layers.occurrenceRole: Relative pronoun identifying ذَٰلِكَ and introducing the clause يَدُعُّ ٱلْيَتِيمَ.

morphology.notes: This repeated occurrence keeps its own sentence role even though the shared teaching identity is the same.

layers.grammar: Masculine singular relative pronoun functioning as the identifier of ذَٰلِكَ and introducing يَدُعُّ ٱلْيَتِيمَ.
learnerConnections: Use ٱلَّذِى after a demonstrative to hear the pattern that is the one who...
Expect the following verb clause to supply the identifying action.

pedagogy.recognitionClue: After ذَٰلِكَ, read ٱلَّذِى as the one who and look for the action that follows.
pedagogy.explanation: Here the relative pronoun does not repeat the person; it identifies that person by the action of repulsing the orphan.
pedagogy.takeaway: ٱلَّذِى = the one who, introducing the identifying action

teaching.rootPicture: The doubled final ع gives the verb a compact, forceful sound that suits pushing or repelling away.
teaching.construction: Imperfect verb with the third-person prefix يـ and a doubled final root consonant: يَدُعُّ.
teaching.grammar: Imperfect indicative, active voice, third person masculine singular; it is the predicate of the relative clause and takes ٱلْيَتِيمَ as its direct object.
teaching.sentenceRole: Predicate of the relative clause introduced by ٱلَّذِى.
teaching.recognitionClue: The initial يـ marks he in the imperfect, and the shadda on the final ع signals the doubled final radical.

forms.difference: The final doubled radical is retained in the imperfect يَدُعُّ and helps convey the forceful action.

teaching.takeaway: يَدُعُّ depicts the harsh rejection of the orphan that the passage condemns.

layers.occurrenceRole: Predicate of the relative clause, taking ٱلْيَتِيمَ as its direct object.

morphology.pattern: فَعَّ / Form I with doubled final radical
morphology.notes: The translation can range from pushes away to repulses; the exact force is contextual and should remain reviewable.

layers.grammar: Imperfect indicative, third person masculine singular, active verb; its direct object is ٱلْيَتِيمَ.
learnerConnections: Recognize يـ as the third-person masculine singular imperfect prefix.
Notice the final shadda as a clue that the final root consonant is doubled.

pedagogy.recognitionClue: Look for يـ at the front and the doubled ع at the end.
pedagogy.explanation: The word is kept atomic because its force is best learned through the complete verb shape; the following noun supplies its direct object.

teaching.rootPicture: The root ي-ت-م is associated with being solitary or without a parent, giving orphan its central image.
teaching.construction: ٱلْ + يَتِيمَ: the definite article followed by the noun يَتِيمَ.
teaching.grammar: Definite masculine singular noun in the accusative; it is the direct object of يَدُعُّ.
teaching.sentenceRole: Direct object receiving the action of being pushed away or repulsed.
teaching.recognitionClue: ٱلْ marks definiteness, and the final fatḥa on يَتِيمَ marks the accusative direct-object ending here.
teaching.takeaway: ٱلْيَتِيمَ is the vulnerable person who is being rejected in the scene.

layers.occurrenceRole: Direct object of يَدُعُّ, the orphan being pushed away or repulsed.

morphology.notes: The final fatḥa is the accusative ending in this occurrence; the article is preserved as a separate meaningful surface component.

layers.grammar: Definite masculine singular accusative noun functioning as the direct object of يَدُعُّ.
learnerConnections: Recognize ٱلْ as the definite article before a sun-letter-free noun.
Use the final fatḥa to identify the noun as the direct object of the verb.

pedagogy.recognitionClue: Split ٱلْيَتِيمَ into ٱلْ + يَتِيمَ and notice the final fatḥa.
pedagogy.explanation: The noun is definite and receives the action of يَدُعُّ, so its accusative ending is visible at the end.
